passage: I'm Vinita, and I sit next to Tejas in Class 5. In the first fractions test he got 4 out of 20. He looked at it for a long time. In the second test he got 6. Ma'am wrote "Practise more!" in red. After that, I noticed he stopped raising his hand in maths. He drew cars in the margin while we did adding fractions. On Monday Ma'am asked him to come to the board and find three-quarters of twelve. He stood there and said, "I'm just not a maths person. My brain doesn't do it." Everyone went quiet. He sat down with his ears red. At lunch he told me he isn't going to try anymore because it's no use. I don't think he's stupid. He's the best at building things in craft class.

qa.q: What did Tejas get in the first fractions test?
qa.a: He got 4 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Tejas decide trying was 'no use'?
qa.a: Tejas felt discouraged and ashamed after failing test after test, ears going red at the board, so he concluded his brain just doesn't do maths and effort is pointless.

qa.q: What small experience could help Tejas start trying again?
qa.a: A teacher could give him fractions through something he's good at, like cutting shapes in craft, so he gets a few right and sees himself improve.

qa.q: How does Vinita see Tejas differently from how he sees himself?
qa.a: Vinita doesn't think he is stupid and notices he's the best at building things, while Tejas has decided he's 'not a maths person'.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy fail fractions repeatedly, decide he is not a maths person and stop trying.

passage:
Monday: Omkar did his fractions homework slowly, tongue between his teeth. The next day it came back with six red crosses out of eight.
Thursday: The new worksheet stayed in his bag. When Tushar, his older brother, asked about it, Omkar said, "Why bother? I'm dumb at fractions. I'll get them all wrong anyway." He went to play carrom instead.
The next Sunday: Tushar drew a round roti on paper and cut it into four. "If you eat one piece, how much is gone?" Omkar rolled his eyes. "One out of four. Obviously." "That's a quarter. You just did a fraction." Omkar blinked. "Do another one," he said, and pulled his chair closer.

qa.q: How many red crosses did Omkar's homework come back with?
qa.a: Six red crosses out of eight.

qa.q: Why did Omkar say 'Why bother?' on Thursday?
qa.a: After so many red crosses, he believed he was dumb at fractions, so trying again felt like signing up for another failure.

qa.q: What choice by Tushar got Omkar trying again, and why?
qa.a: Tushar used a paper roti so Omkar got an easy one right, a taste of success that made him ask for another.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt seeing the worksheet stay in the bag?
qa.a: Tushar was probably worried his brother was giving up, which may be why he tried a different, easier way on Sunday.

grounding: Over a week, a boy gives up on fractions after repeated failure until one small success restarts his effort.

passage: Sarika, you think you're bad at fractions? Your Irawati aaji was worse. When I was a girl of ten, in our school in Satara, I got every fraction sum wrong for a whole term. Half plus a third, three-quarters of something, all wrong. The teacher sighed each time she handed back my slate. After a while I decided I had a "wrong brain" for numbers. I stopped even copying the sums. I'd sit and draw rangoli patterns in my notebook instead. My mother thought I was lazy. It was my uncle, the tailor, who changed it. He had me cut cloth: "Give me three-quarters of this metre." I got it right. Then again. I remember that feeling, like a door opening. But for two years before that, I simply didn't try.

qa.q: What did Irawati draw instead of copying the sums?
qa.a: She drew rangoli patterns in her notebook instead.

qa.q: Why did young Irawati decide she had a 'wrong brain' for numbers?
qa.a: After getting every fraction wrong for a whole term with no sign of improving, she concluded she simply couldn't do it, so trying felt useless.

qa.q: What did the uncle choose to do differently, and why did it work?
qa.a: He gave her fractions through cutting cloth, a real task where she could get it right, so she finally experienced getting better.

qa.q: Why might Irawati aaji's mother have thought she was lazy?
qa.a: From outside, a child drawing rangoli instead of doing sums looks lazy, but inside Irawati had given up after failing again and again.

grounding: A grandmother recalls failing fractions until she believed she could not do maths and stopped trying.

passage:
The house was full of cousins for Pinky didi's wedding, the dholak going in the courtyard, and Gurpreet sat on the stairs with the fractions worksheet. Third test this month: 3 out of 20. The one before, 5. The one before that, 4.
He tried the first sum again: 2/3 + 1/4. He added the tops and added the bottoms. It looked wrong. It always looked wrong.
Nirmala Aunty, the tuition teacher from next door, came up the stairs with a plate of laddoos. 'Show me where you're stuck.'
Gurpreet folded the worksheet into a tiny square. 'I'm just not a maths person. Everyone knows.'
'Who's everyone?'
He shrugged and went down to the courtyard, where nobody asked about fractions. The folded square stayed on the step.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet score on the third fractions test?
qa.a: 3 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet say 'I'm just not a maths person'?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels ashamed and hopeless after three failed tests, so he has decided the problem is him rather than the method, and trying feels pointless.

qa.q: What choice could Nirmala Aunty make next to rebuild Gurpreet's motivation?
qa.a: She could sit with him on one sum, find the single step that goes wrong, and let him get that step right a few times, so he feels himself improving.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty feel seeing the folded worksheet left on the step?
qa.a: She may feel concerned, seeing that he hasn't just failed fractions but given up on himself, and wonder how to reach him.

grounding: A child who keeps failing fractions decides he is not a maths person and stops trying.

passage:
In Class 6 at the school near Tolichowki, Naveen had stopped even copying down the fraction sums. When Ma'am wrote 3/5 of 20 on the board, he drew a cricket bat in the margin instead.
'Try it,' whispered Wasim, his bench partner.
'What's the point? I got the last four wrong. My brain doesn't do fractions.'
At home in their flat, he left the maths homework for last and then 'forgot' it. Ammi signed the teacher's note in his diary without a word.
On Friday Wasim tried again, cutting his tiffin roti into five pieces. 'Look. Three of these five. Easy.'
Naveen looked at the roti for a second, almost interested. Then he pushed it back. 'For you, maybe.'

qa.q: What did Naveen draw in the margin instead of doing the sum?
qa.a: A cricket bat.

qa.q: What does Naveen's 'For you, maybe' suggest about how he sees himself?
qa.a: It suggests he feels discouraged and sure he simply can't do fractions; after four wrong answers, even an easy example feels meant for others, not for him.

qa.q: What was the almost-turning point, and what could help it stick?
qa.a: Naveen looking at the roti slices, almost interested; if Wasim or Ma'am let him solve one very easy sum right then, a small success could start to rebuild his belief.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel when Naveen pushes the roti back?
qa.a: Wasim may feel disappointed after trying twice to help a friend, and unsure how to get through.

passage: In Class 5B, Miss Rao wrote fractions on the board: add one-third and one-quarter. Hemant copied it, stared, and wrote two-sevenths. Wrong again, the fourth time this week. His notebook was all red crosses. When Miss Rao gave the next sum, he didn't pick up his pencil. Akash nudged him. 'Try. It's like pizza slices.' Hemant shook his head. 'I'm just bad at maths. My brain can't do it.' He drew a small car in the margin instead. When Miss Rao came past, he covered the page with his arm. For the rest of the period he looked out of the window at the crows on the wire, and didn't try a single sum.

passage:
Monday. Pooja got 3 out of 20 in the fractions test. The one before, 5. The one before that, 4. She folded the paper very small and pushed it to the bottom of her bag.
Wednesday. Her brother Sahil offered to help with the homework. 'Fractions are easy once you get the trick.' 'Not for me,' Pooja said. 'I'm a maths duffer. Everyone knows.' She did her English homework twice instead, very neatly.
Friday. In class, when the teacher put up a fraction sum, Pooja didn't even copy it. She drew a border of flowers round her page and waited for the bell. That evening Sahil found the folded test and sat beside her. 'Let's do just one,' he said. 'The smallest one.' She shrugged, but she didn't leave.

qa.q: What did Pooja score on Monday's fractions test?
qa.a: She scored 3 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Pooja do her English homework twice instead of maths?
qa.a: After repeated low marks she felt ashamed and hopeless about maths, so she turned to a subject where she felt able.

qa.q: What is wise about Sahil's 'just one, the smallest one'?
qa.a: A tiny, doable sum gives Pooja a chance to feel herself getting something right, which can start to rebuild motivation.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel finding the folded test?
qa.a: Sahil might feel sad and protective, realising his sister has given up, and want to help without pressure.

grounding: Over a week, a child who keeps failing fractions decides she is a maths duffer and stops trying, until her brother offers one small step.

passage: Divyansh, you say you're just stupid at fractions. Your Preeti Dadi said the same thing, long ago, in a village school near Meerut. Every week the master wrote fractions on the blackboard, and every week I got them wrong. After a month I stopped trying. I sat at the back drawing mango trees on my slate, telling myself some people are born stupid at sums. Then a new teacher came, Kamla Behenji. She didn't give me the hard sums. She gave me a roti and asked me to break it into four. Then take one piece. 'What part is that?' 'A quarter.' 'Correct.' My first correct answer in months. The next day, two rotis. By the end of term I was helping the girl beside me. I wasn't stupid. I had just never once felt myself getting better.

qa.q: What did Kamla Behenji ask Preeti to break into four?
qa.a: She asked Preeti to break a roti into four.

qa.q: Why did Preeti stop trying after a month?
qa.a: She got fractions wrong every week and felt ashamed and hopeless, believing she was simply born stupid at sums.

qa.q: What turning point in the story brought Preeti's motivation back?
qa.a: Kamla Behenji's roti lesson gave her a first correct answer, and small daily wins let her feel herself getting better.

qa.q: How might Kamla Behenji have seen the girl drawing mango trees?
qa.a: She likely saw a child who had lost hope, not a stupid one, and started with something Preeti could succeed at.

grounding: A grandmother recalls giving up on fractions as a child after repeated failure, until small wins let her feel herself improving.

passage:
Gargi's cousin's wedding was in four days, and the house was chaos: relatives on every mattress, a band practising next door, pressure cookers whistling.
Gargi, ten, sat in a corner with her fractions homework. Three-quarters plus one-half. She got 4/6. Wrong. She tried again. Wrong again. Yesterday's test had come back with a big red 3 out of 20.
Her brother Chinmay leaned over. “Common denominator, remember?”
“I don't remember. I never remember.” She shut the notebook. “I'm just stupid at maths.”
“You're not…”
“I am. Every time I try, it's wrong. So why try?”
She pushed the book under the mattress and went to watch the mehendi. Chinmay looked at the notebook, then at her, and didn't know what to say.

qa.q: Why did Gargi decide there was no point trying?

qa.q: How could someone help Gargi start feeling able again?
qa.a: A patient adult could sit with her in a quiet spot and work through very easy fraction steps, so she experiences small successes.

qa.q: What is it like for Chinmay to hear his sister call herself stupid?
qa.a: Chinmay feels worried and helpless, wanting to comfort her but not knowing what to say.

passage:
Parveen's maths notebook was full of red crosses. Fractions. Again.
In the Lucknow tuition centre, Sumit Sir had drawn pizzas on the board. Everyone else nodded. Parveen stared. Why did two-eighths equal one-quarter? It didn't look equal.
She tried the first worksheet. Wrong. The second. Wrong. At the third, she stopped writing and drew a cat in the margin.
“Parveen, try question four,” Sumit Sir said.
“I can't do maths, Sir.” She said it calmly, as if it were a fact, like her name.
“You can learn this.”
“No. My brain isn't a maths brain. Ammi says she was bad at it too.”
She didn't open the worksheet again for the rest of the class. The red crosses stayed on the page.

qa.a: He had drawn pizzas on the board.

“Lalremsiami, your homework?”
“I didn't do it, Papa.”
“Why?”
“Fractions.”
Amandeep sat beside her on the bed. “What about fractions?”
“I got every question wrong in class. Every one. Pu Lalthanga said to practise. I practised. Still wrong.”
“How many did you try?”
“Ten. All wrong.” She pulled her knees up. “I'm not a maths person, Papa. Some people just aren't.”
“You were good at sums last year.”
“That was sums. This is fractions. I'm not doing any more.”
“Not even one with me?”
She shook her head and turned toward the wall. “What's the point? It'll be wrong.”
Amandeep looked at the notebook. Ten crosses, neat and careful. She had really tried.

passage:
The summer I was ten, fractions beat me every day. Pranav bhaiya would give me a sum, and I'd get it wrong. Again. Again. After two weeks I said, "I can't do maths. I'm just bad at it." I stopped trying. When he gave me a sum, I'd write any answer just to finish.
Then one afternoon he did something new. He cut a roti into four pieces and asked me to give him one quarter. Easy. Then two quarters. "That's a half," I said. He grinned. "You just did fractions." The next day, a pizza drawing with eighths. I got it right. And the next. Each small win made me want to try the next one.
I wasn't bad at maths. I'd just never felt myself get better at it.
— Shreya

qa.q: What did Pranav bhaiya cut into four pieces?
qa.a: He cut a roti into four pieces.

qa.q: Why did Shreya stop trying at fractions?
qa.a: After failing again and again, Shreya felt defeated and decided maths was impossible, so there seemed no point in trying.

qa.q: What did Pranav bhaiya do that brought back Shreya's effort?
qa.a: He used a roti and drawings to give easy, winnable steps, so Shreya could feel improvement and want to try again.

qa.q: How might Pranav bhaiya have felt when Shreya said "That's a half"?
qa.a: He was probably happy and relieved to see Shreya succeed.

grounding: A child recalls failing at fractions until deciding maths was impossible, and how small experiences of getting better restored motivation.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Onam week, by Jomon
Gargi, Class 4, has failed four fraction tests in a row. Today, while the others made pookalam designs, her maths book stayed closed. "I'm stupid at maths," she said. "Why try?" She didn't even write her name on the worksheet.
She hasn't had one success in fractions all term, so she has stopped trying.
I asked her to help me share the flowers for the pookalam among four groups. She divided them carefully. "Each group gets one quarter," I said. She blinked. "That's fractions?" "That's fractions." She smiled a little.
What I did next: I've made her a set of very short fraction cards, one step at a time, each one she can get right. She'll do three a day and tick them off herself.

qa.q: How many fraction tests has Gargi failed in a row?
qa.a: Gargi has failed four fraction tests in a row.

qa.q: Why did Gargi keep her maths book closed?
qa.a: Gargi felt defeated, calling herself stupid at maths, because she had never had one success in fractions all term.

qa.q: What plan did Jomon make, and why could it restore Gargi's motivation?
qa.a: Short fraction cards she can get right, three a day, so she can see herself getting better.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Gargi asked, "That's fractions?"
qa.a: Jomon was probably hopeful and pleased, seeing Gargi smile at her first success in a long time.

grounding: A teacher's festival-week note shows a girl who fails fractions repeatedly and stops trying, and a plan to give her experiences of getting better.

passage:
Diwali holidays, Tuesday
Jaya didi tried to help me with fractions again. I got the first three wrong. So I closed the book and said, "Forget it. I can't do maths. I'm too dumb."
Didi didn't argue. She took the box of sweets Nani sent and put it on the table. "There are twelve kaju katlis. If you get one third, how many?" I counted. "Four." "Correct. You just did a fraction." I laughed. Then she asked for one quarter. Three. Right again.
I got eight right in a row, and ate one sweet for each.
I still hate the book. But I think maybe I'm not dumb. I think I just never got enough right to feel it.
Tomorrow Didi said we'll do it with the diyas.
Nilesh

qa.q: How many kaju katlis were in the box?
qa.a: There were twelve kaju katlis.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel before and after the sweets game?
qa.a: Before, Nilesh felt dumb and defeated after three wrong answers; after getting eight right in a row, Nilesh felt maybe not dumb after all.

qa.q: Why did Jaya didi's sweets game work?
qa.a: It gave Nilesh easy, real wins in a row, so the experience of getting better brought back motivation.

qa.q: How might Jaya didi feel reading this diary, if she ever did?
qa.a: She would probably feel happy and proud that her game helped Nilesh believe in doing maths.

grounding: A child's festival diary shows feeling too dumb for fractions after repeated failure, until small wins with sweets restore motivation.

passage:
Harvest time in Chandrika's village near Mandya meant the school was half empty, children away cutting paddy with their families. In the quiet classroom, Parul Teacher wrote four fraction sums on the board.
Chandrika got the first one wrong. And the second. She had got them wrong last week too, and the week before. When the third sum came, she didn't even pick up her slate pencil.
"Try, Chandrika," Parul Teacher said.
"I can't do maths. My brain is not a maths brain." She pushed the slate away. "Amma also can't do maths."
That evening, at the family's vegetable stall, she sold two bunches of coriander and gave back the exact change. She didn't notice she had done a sum at all.

qa.q: Why does Chandrika say "My brain is not a maths brain"?

qa.q: What could Parul Teacher try?
qa.a: Start Chandrika on easier fraction sums she can get right, show her how she improves, and link fractions to things she already does, like giving change at the stall.
